title: Ask HN: How do people self host email and maintain deliverability?
summary:
I wanted to self host my email and decided to rent a VPS. I made sure the ipv4 address was on no blacklist. My domain uses a good TLD with a long domain history. I set up SPF, DKIM, DMARC, reverse IP DNS, etc.

I sent 3 emails to my personal outlook/hotmail accounts, all of which went to spam. 1 day later, my IP was banned. Outlook support said they cannot discuss the reason for the ban and will not unban it so I'm out of luck.

I know I can just pay a provider $5/month and get email, but there is something about having full control over your own email. Is there anything much I can do?

title: 12 Angry Agents
summary:
12 angry men is a very thought-provoking film, and there is nothing quite like it. Its premise is just 12 people sitting in the jury room and sharing their experiences and judgment on a very sensitive case. They need to decide whether a boy is innocent or guilty of a crime.

I have been playing around with a thought experiment where agents play human roles and come to a conclusion. I created agents for each jury, and the judge is another agent that can make an informed decision based on what the juries come up with. I fed the movie script into the setup, and each jury uses the Recall tools to refine their belief, and how they came to a conclusion.

I built this using Polign Recall - https://github.com/Polign/recall , langGraph and agent-sandbox.

1. Each jury agent processes the conversation in its own terms.

2. The memory gets folded, and contradiction and change of mind get processed as part of their own belief system.

3. The judge decides how each juror finally concluded their belief and whether they came to be with an informed decision or were coerced into the decision.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Here is the conclusion by the judge (This is AI generated for a reason) -

As the judge, I'd rule: not guilty, and the verdict stands. The prosecution's case was meant to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and each piece of it fails once tested in the jury room:

The knife isn't unique. Juror 8 bought an identical switchblade in the boy's neighborhood, so the "one of a kind" weapon ties no one to the killing.

The old man couldn't have seen the boy run. He had had a stroke and drags one leg. Walked out in the jury room, he couldn't reach his door in the 15 seconds he claimed.

The woman across the street wasn't wearing her glasses. She had marks on her nose from glasses, and she saw the stabbing from bed, at night, through the windows of a passing train. She wouldn't have been wearing them in bed. "I'm going to kill you" couldn't be heard. The train was passing at that moment, and it's loud enough to drown out speech.

The stab wound doesn't fit. The wound angled downward, but someone experienced with a switchblade stabs underhand. A shorter boy stabbing downward at a taller man is unlikely. The boy forgetting the movie proves little. Juror 3, sitting calmly in the jury room, can't remember a film he saw days earlier.

Did the boy kill his father? Neither the film nor the record answers that, and a judge doesn't rule on it. A judge rules on whether the state proved its case. On this record it didn't: every eyewitness account and every piece of physical evidence fails. Not guilty is the definite answer the evidence supports.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The premise behind the memory updates and storage-

A change of mind is a correction: When a later scene changes what a juror believes, Recall keeps the newer belief as current and keeps the older one as what it replaced, with the scene it came from. A juror who moves from guilty to not guilty carries both beliefs, the scene where each began, and the scene where the first one ended. Recall's diff returns exactly what started and stopped being believed in the final act.

Opinions from memory alone: At the end, each juror is asked what they make of the outcome. The model gets that juror's memory from Recall, and not the script. It answers in the juror's voice and cites the scene behind every belief. If a juror was misled and never found out, they still believe it.

A conclusion from separate minds: The last step reads the final pages and every juror's memory, side by side, and names the question the film leaves open. It answers that question with evidence that names the juror and the remembered scene, for example, a late change of mind, or something one juror knows that another does not. Because each memory was kept apart, the conclusion can see where the jurors disagree.

title: Tell HN: Claude CLI doesn't exit anymore, not even with CTRL-C
summary:
So I found myself surprised today that exiting the CLI with CTRL-C does not, in fact, close Claude CLI. What it does is it closes the agent's terminal interface, but it leaves a background process active, even if you didn't work on anything at all.

Try it yourself: run claude, exit to main conversations list, close it immediately with CTRL-C or /exit, then `ps ax|grep claude`.

Apparently it's not a bug, it's a "feature", introduced earlier this year. You need to disable Agent View (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-view, disableAgentView in settings.json) to stop that behavior. But then you lose the ability to open the list all your chats in main view, effectively crippling it.

This is yet another frustrating anti-pattern they introduce and it personally upsets me that 5 decades of established paradigms (CTRL-C is CTRL-C!) continue to be thrown out of the window just like that.

I guess at 30k changes a day you kinda have to fell entitled to not care about anything legacy.

EDIT: you can still show a list of chats with disableAgentView, just need an explicit `claude --resume`. It's a different UI, but with an actual search!

Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50214693

title: Ask HN: How can I grow as an engineer in the AI era
summary:
I'm a junior developer, with less than 1 yoe. I have to use AI at work because deadlines are tight, and if I try to solve something by myself, it would take too much time. Work has to be done like yesterday. I'm trying not to use AI when I fix some bugs because they don't have such tight deadlines, but I feel so behind when it takes too long.

As you can probably guess, AI is destroying me on different levels. It often creates much better solutions than I do because I don't know this large codebase well. It can write code without forgetting to add something somewhere. But sometimes I can see that the suggested solution is bad, and I argue with a soulless machine about it.

I don't know much. My solutions are too straightforward and stupid. I can't make architectural and design decisions, or the ones I make are simply bad. I can't sit down and describe how I'm going to solve something because I don't know what might come up when I start. And I'm trying not to feed slop to PR reviewers, and I truly learn something when they suggest something to me.

I want to be a good engineer, and I thought that if I started working, it would come to me naturally. But now I'm in this LLM loop where everyone is expected to use AI, yet it gives me nothing in terms of real experience, and people don't want to teach anyone anymore.

I don't know what to do. I want to become a good engineer even if this profession won't exist, and now my life and my family depend on my income, so I can't just decide "It's not for me".

What should I do? Spend my free time trying to understand the codebase without AI? Try to create something myself without AI? Improve my problem-solving skills, learn new things from books, practice implementation?

title: Ask HN: Is the downside of investing in AI real?
summary:
Some global tech leaders believe that investing in AI is an imperative. However, they should bear the following in mind:

- Every time AI is used, it costs the AI providers money in processing power, electricity, and cooling. To capture market share, they are currently charging less than the actual cost of providing the service, and if prices were to rise, using it would become less profitable.

- Many AI projects yield no results because companies struggle to adapt their workflows, or because they fail to properly measure costs and benefits, despite the technology being highly capable.

- AI equipment and chips become nearly obsolete in just 3 to 4 years, whereas infrastructure takes 10 to 20 years to pay off; furthermore, maintaining this infrastructure can cost more than the profits it is expected to generate.

Therefore, is it wise to carefully evaluate whether integrating AI truly makes sense for companies? In doing so, would their AI investments be more deliberate and efficient, generating both economic and productivity benefits?

Customers who have connected Zapier to Unbounce: Zapier connects to Unbounce through Unbounce’s API using OAuth. On October 22, Unbounce revoked all existing tokens for these connections. No further action is needed. Customers may remove Unbounce from My Apps in Zapier.

Customers who have used an API key: No action is needed within Unbounce.

title: Ask HN: When can we trust AI in coding, and avoid the happy path issue?
summary:
I have a question, and I hope you can clarify it. Consider this scenario: Claude code runs on a desktop to develop a solution, and its directive requires Codex to test everything it does under a different directive. The Codex directive is to refute Claude's test results, maintain its own test ledger, and return PASS or NO PASS. Claude cannot negotiate; it has to fix the NO PASS issues. Even with such a strict environment, I am ending up with problems, and of course, when asking Claude, the answer is "This is on me; I did not do X and Y"; when I ask it whether Codex checked it, "Codex checked all but not this "...

So when can we trust the AI to do the full job, not just the happy path? Is there a better way to impose quality?

I feel that on large projects, even if I upload Claude directives to re-read, Claude or Codex (we can switch roles) tends to drift and miss things.

Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50209084

title: Kernal.org Compromised?
summary:
It might give some of you a Friday laugh - but it nearly gave me a heart attack. I'm building a kernel appliance and while it was building I thought to check the kernel website, but autocomplete sent me to kernal.org instead of kernel.org. I had a moment of sheer panic - with all these CVE's recently anything is possible.

I wonder what the history behind kernal.org is? It is some kind of troll for linux heads?
